% A minipage cannot break across leaves: it overruns in silence. So every unit is
% boxed, its height written out, and only then set — python compares the height
% against \textheight. This is the measurement the mirror got from page marks.
\newcommand{\originals}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue
      \setnoted{}#3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  % ⚠ \ht0 ALONE IS WRONG HERE and silently reported ~5.7pt for every Part I
  % verso until 2026-08-09. This vbox's content is ONE LINE of two tall boxes, so
  % its height is just that line's height above the baseline and the whole column
  % sits in the DEPTH. Measure ht+dp. (\originalsone and \enleaf are multi-line
  % vboxes and were never affected.)
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0\relax}\box0}

\newcommand{\originalsone}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

\newcommand{\enleaf}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

% ---- the two foot-bands -------------------------------------------------
% The Loeb leaves roughly 44% of every leaf empty, and a Loeb's foot is where an
% apparatus belongs. The verso band carries the apparatus criticus against the
% originals; the recto band carries explanatory notes against the English.
%
% ⚠ The band is set at the FOOT, which means the leaf must be composed as a box
% of exactly \textheight with \vfill between body and band. \vfil alone will not
% do it: the preamble sets \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with it
% and lands the band a third of the way up. Same trap as the display leaves.
%
% ⚠ The band is measured INTO the fit record (\dimexpr body + band), not beside
% it. A band that overruns is exactly as silent as a minipage that overruns, and
% the point of the instrument is that nothing is unmeasured — which is how Part
% I's verso went 131 leaves without ever being tested.
% ⚠ The \par after the rule is load-bearing: without it the rule is just an inline
% box and the band's first word sets on the same line as the rule.
\newcommand{\bandrule}{\par\vspace{5pt}%
  {\noindent\color{rulegray}\rule{0.28\textwidth}{0.4pt}\par}\vspace{3.5pt}}

\newcommand{\apparatusband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\scriptsize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{1pt}%
    \raggedright #1\par}}

\newcommand{\notesband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\footnotesize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{2pt}%
    #1\par}}

% Compose a leaf whose body sits at the top and whose band sits at the foot.
\newcommand{\bandleaf}[2]{\vbox to \textheight{#1\vfill#2}}

% #5 = the Latin column's own noted lines, #6 = how many romans the Greek column
% already spent, so the series runs on rather than restarting at i.
\newcommand{\originalsn}[6]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      % ⚠ numbered on ITS OWN count — see the preamble. It is NOT reliably
      % line-for-line with the Greek: 20 of Part I's 131 openings differ, by as
      % much as six lines, because the plate turns its own long lines.
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}%
      \setnotedcol{#5}{#6}\plreset\plnumtrue #3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\originalsonen}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\enleafn}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\notesband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

% Place a display block a fixed way down the leaf. NOT \vfil: the preamble sets
% \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with any \vfil pair and lands the
% block about a third of the way down by accident. A title page sits where it is
% put, so put it.
\newcommand{\dropto}[1]{\vspace*{#1\textheight}}

% A leaf composed as one box of exactly the text height, so \vfill inside it
% divides the leaf instead of competing with \raggedbottom's bottom glue.
\newcommand{\fullleaf}[1]{\thispagestyle{empty}%
  \vbox to \textheight{#1}\clearpage}

% A display leaf: the 1853's own title and half-title pages, which are not running

% indent and centre, so the fragment renders as the page it is.
\newcommand{\titleleaf}[2]{\thispagestyle{empty}%

    \renewcommand{\parasep}{\par\vspace{2.4\baselineskip}}%
    \renewcommand{\pl}[2]{\par{\Large\scshape ##2}}%
    #2\par
  \endgroup}

\enleafn{2}{\input{fragments/en002}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Luke xviii. 1 — \emph{men ought always to pray, and not to faint} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,1 Thess. v. 17 — \emph{pray without ceasing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Dan. vi. 10 — Daniel kneeling three times a day, as he did aforetime \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxix. 164 — \emph{seven times a day do I praise thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gen. xxiv. 63 — Isaac going out to meditate at the eventide \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxix. 62 — \emph{at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ex. xx. 24 — \emph{in all places where I record my name I will come unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxi. 1 — \emph{in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{The canonical hours, built out of Scripture rather than out of a breviary.} \emph{Seven times a day do I praise thee} sets the number, and each of the seven is then given a text that shows somebody praying at that hour: Mark's \emph{a great while before day}, the psalmist's morning watches, the third hour at Pentecost, Peter's sixth hour on the housetop, the ninth hour at the Beautiful Gate, Isaac at eventide, the night watches — with midnight added from the same psalm that set the number. \textbf{The office is being derived, not inherited}, and that is the argument of the whole opening.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{4}{\input{fragments/en004}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. vi. 6 — \emph{enter into thy closet, and shut thy door} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts x. 9 — Peter praying on the housetop \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts iii. 1 — Peter and John going up into the temple \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Acts xxi. 5 — kneeling down on the shore, at parting \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxlix. 5 — \emph{let them sing aloud upon their beds} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Mark i. 35 — \emph{a solitary place, and there prayed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. ii. 8 — \emph{that men pray every where} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xcix. 6 — \emph{Samuel among them that call upon his name}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{And the places, by the same method as the hours opposite.} The closet, the housetop, the temple, the sea-shore, the bed, the wilderness — each a place where somebody in Scripture is found praying — and then \emph{every where}, which is not a seventh place but the conclusion drawn from the six.}

\enleafn{24}{\input{fragments/en024}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xcv. 8 — \emph{harden not your heart}; Heb. iii. 13 — \emph{lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xci. 6 — the Vulgate's \emph{noonday demon}, where the BCP has \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Matt. vi. 34 — \emph{sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. lxxviii. 33 — \emph{their years in trouble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xix. 2 — \emph{day unto day uttereth speech} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxliii. 8 — \emph{for I lift up my soul unto thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Two lines here take the Vulgate against the Prayer Book, and the English follows the Vulgate.} \emph{Negotium perambulans in tenebris} and \emph{dæmonium meridianum} — the business that walks in darkness and the noonday demon — are what Andrewes wrote; Coverdale has \emph{pestilence} and \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day}. CONVENTIONS §9 makes the BCP our crib, and yields wherever he reaches past it, as he does here.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,⚠⚠ \textbf{This is the verse Part III mis-numbers, and here the volume gets it right.} \emph{Anni mei in luctu} stands at printed \textbf{409} under \textup{Psal. xl. 9}, where the note has to say the reference is wrong; here the same half-verse is referred correctly to \textbf{\textup{Ps. lxxviii. 33}}. So the edition proves its own misprint across three hundred and eighty pages — and it confirms, from inside the book, a reading that was otherwise established only from Brightman. \textbf{Both kept as printed.}}

\enleafn{32}{\input{fragments/en032}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 20 — the epistle's closing blessing, on the God who brought again the great Shepherd \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ex. xxxiv. 6 — the LORD proclaiming his own Name to Moses in the cleft of the rock; Num. xiv. 18 — Moses pleading that same Name after the spies \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. vii. 24 — \emph{O wretched man that I am} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Jon. ii. 8 — Jonah out of the fish's belly: \emph{they that observe lying vanities} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxli. 4 — the plate marks its reading as the Septuagint's \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Josh. vii. 19 — Joshua to Achan: \emph{give glory to the LORD, and make confession} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxxii. 5 — \emph{I acknowledged my sin unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Josh. vii. 20 — Achan's answer: \emph{indeed I have sinned} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. viii. 6 — \emph{no man repented him, saying, What have I done?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{Both halves of the exchange at Ai, three lines apart.} Joshua charges Achan to \emph{give glory to the LORD and make confession}; Achan answers \emph{thus and thus have I done}. Here the charge and the confession are alike the penitent's own words, with Ps. xxxii. 5 set between them — neither half meaning in the prayer what it meant in the history. The re-cutting is the composition.}

\originalsn{34}{\input{fragments/gr034}}{\input{fragments/la035}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,27 \textup{Τὰ ἔργα}] \textup{τὸ πλάσμα} \emph{apogr.} — \emph{cf. Lat.} \textup{Figmenta}, \emph{quod ex neutro fonte alio fluere potest}\\[1pt]\hphantom{x}27–28 \emph{punct. post} \textup{παριδῇς} \emph{del. apogr.} · \textup{ὁμοίωμα}] \textup{ὁμοίωμα.} \emph{apogr.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,27 \textup{Figmenta}] \emph{Vulg.} \textup{opera manuum tuarum}; \emph{ex Gr.} \textup{πλάσμα} \emph{pendet, non ex textu impresso}}{27}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{34}
\setnoted{1,6,7,9,13,16,20,23,27,29}
\enleafn{34}{\input{fragments/en034}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xxxiii. 27 — Elihu, on the man brought back from the pit \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. ii. 1 — to the man who judges another and does the same; [Tit. iii. 11] — \emph{condemned of himself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Hos. xiii. 9 — the LORD to Israel: \emph{thou hast destroyed thyself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Dan. ix. 7 — Daniel in the exile, at the evening sacrifice \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Neh. ix. 33 — the Levites' confession, while the Law is read \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxxix. 7 — David, having first been dumb with silence \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxxxix. 46 — Ethan: how short a time God has made men for \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Cor. vi. 20 — \emph{ye are bought with a price} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. lxxxix. 47 — \emph{wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{The Greek and the Latin part company in the first line.} The Greek says \emph{thou hast chastened me for the things wherein I sinned}; the Latin gives \emph{Non recepi} and refers it to Job xxxiii. 27, \emph{it profited me not}. They are not renderings of one another. The English follows the Greek, per CONVENTIONS §6, and the Latin stands as the independent witness it is — see the note at 27 below.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{A pun the English Bible cannot keep.} Andrewes asks \emph{what is my expectation} and answers \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, then four lines later \emph{Memorare quæ mea substantia}. Both are the Vulgate — Ps. xxxviii. 8 and lxxxviii. 48 — and both turn on \textbf{substantia}, which is why the two psalms can be set one on top of the other. The Authorised Version renders the first \emph{my hope is in thee} and the second \emph{remember how short my time is}, and the join disappears.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ix}\,\textup{Figmenta} \textbf{is the evidence that this Latin column is a witness and not a shadow.} The printed Greek reads \emph{the works of thy hands}, and the Vulgate of Ps. cxxxviii. 8 reads \emph{opera manuum tuarum}; the Latin here reads neither. \emph{Figmenta} — the thing moulded — can only render a Greek text that read \textup{τὸ πλάσμα}, which is what the manuscript reads and what the printed page does not.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{42}{\input{fragments/en042}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 7 — \emph{them which have the rule over you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the first promise: the seed that bruises the serpent's head \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Deut. xxxii. 29 — \emph{O that they would consider their latter end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. xx. 6 — the labourers found standing idle in the market-place \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxvi. 4 — \emph{I have not sat with vain persons}; Tit. iii. 10 — a heretic, after the first and second admonition, rejected \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Job xxxi. 1 — \emph{I made a covenant with mine eyes} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Hos. ii. 6 — \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}The Hebrew in the heading — \textup{\RL{סיג התורה}}, \emph{a fence about the Law} — \textbf{is on the printed page}, not supplied; one of the few places the 1853 let Andrewes' Hebrew stand. ⚠ \textbf{And the page ends by quoting the fence.} The last resolution is Hosea's \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}, so a rabbinic phrase for the Law's protective hedge opens the page and a prophet's hedge closes it. \sethead{The Second Day}
% ---------- opening 70 | 71 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{70}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Day}
\originals{70}{\input{fragments/gr070}}{\input{fragments/la071}}
\clearpage
\markright{70}
\setnoted{3,5,13,16,23}
\enleafn{70}{\input{fragments/en070}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. v. 3 — \emph{in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 6 — \textbf{the work of the second day}: the firmament in the midst of the waters \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxlvii. 16 — \emph{he casteth forth his ice like morsels} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxxv. 7 — \emph{he bringeth the wind out of his treasuries} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Lev. xxvi. 40 — \emph{if they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{This is the key to the whole of Part I.} Each of the seven days opens from that day's work in Genesis, and prays out of it: the second day made the firmament, so the second day's prayer begins there and runs down through the waters above the heavens — showers, ice, dew, hail, snow, hoar-frost, winds — before it turns to confession. The days are not seven prayers that happen to fall in a week; they are the week itself, prayed through.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{78}{\input{fragments/en078}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,[Ps. xxxix. 8] — \emph{and my substance is with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxxi. 1 — \emph{let me never be put to confusion}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{The same half-verse is cited twice in this book under two different numbers.} At printed 34 it is \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, referred to \textup{Psal. xxxix. 7}; here it is the same clause referred to \textup{[Psal. xxxix. 8]}. The difference is the numbering, not the text: \textbf{xxxix. 7 is the Authorised Version's figure and xxxix. 8 the Prayer Book's}, which runs one ahead here. And the Prayer Book's figure is the one in \textbf{square brackets} — the 1853 editor's own mark for a reference he supplied. So the plate cites Andrewes' psalm on the AV's numbering and the editor cites it on the BCP's, on two pages of one book. Both stand as printed.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{82}{\input{fragments/en082}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{Andrewes is praying for the places he himself served, under their etymologies.} \emph{The Southern Spring} is \textbf{Southwell} and \emph{the Western Monastery} is \textbf{Westminster}, as the Latin column says outright (\emph{sc. Southwell}, \emph{sc. Westmonasterii}); with St Paul's between them these are his own prebends and his deanery. The English keeps the descriptive form because the Greek does, and the identification sits where Andrewes put it, on the facing page.}

Winton}. ⚠ \textbf{The phrase dates the prayer}: he came to Winchester in 1619 and died in 1626, so this leaf of the Intercession was written, or last revised, in his last seven years. \enleafn{92}{\input{fragments/en092}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xliii. 1 — \emph{O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee}, which opens Psalm lxiii \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 9 — \textbf{the work of the third day}: the waters gathered, and the dry land appearing \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxxiii. 7 — the Septuagint's \emph{as in a wineskin}, where the AV has \emph{as an heap}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{The plate cites \textup{Psal. xliii. 1}, and the verse is Psalm lxiii. 1.} \emph{Ad te de luce vigilo} is the Vulgate of Ps. lxii. 2, the AV's \emph{early will I seek thee}; Ps. xliii. 1 is \emph{judge me, O God, and plead my cause}, which is not this line. The likeliest mechanism is a dropped letter — \textup{xliii} for \textup{lxiii} — the same slip the volume makes at printed 411, where \textup{lxviii} stands for \textup{lxxviii}. Kept as printed.}

\originalsn{96}{\input{fragments/gr096}}{\input{fragments/la097}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,25 \emph{voces Hebrææ Græcis respondentes in altero} στοίχῳ \emph{subjiciuntur apogr.}: \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}}}{}{1}

\markright{96}
\setnoted{7,9,10,11,14,24,25,32}
\enleafn{96}{\input{fragments/en096}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Kings viii. 47 — Solomon at the dedication, praying for those who repent in the land of their captivity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xli. 4 — the verse of line 21 opposite, turned into the third person \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — Paul, \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xv. 18 — the prodigal: \emph{make me as one of thy hired servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxx. 9 — \emph{thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the seven marks of godly sorrow, which this column sets out\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vii}\,⚠ \textbf{Under these seven Greek words for sin the manuscript sets a Hebrew column, and the 1853 left it out.} The apograph gives \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}} — \emph{yetzer, shegagah, asham, ḥaṭṭa'ah, pesha, avon, to'evah}, the standard rabbinic vocabulary of sin, set as a lexicon beneath the Greek. \textbf{It is not in the printed book at all.} ⚠ And the first of them is the word Andrewes glosses \textup{\RL{יצר טוב}}, the good inclination, at printed 76: so his \emph{φαντασία} is being read through the rabbinic doctrine of the two inclinations, which is a fact about his theology and not a footnote about his text. Recorded here; not restored to the page.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{102}{\input{fragments/en102}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. vii. 24 — \emph{O wretched man that I am} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Sam. vii. 28 — David after the promise: \emph{thou art that God, and thy words be true} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. v. 20 — \emph{where sin abounded, grace did much more abound} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Tit. iii. 4 — \emph{the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Cor. x. 1 — \emph{the meekness and gentleness of Christ} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. ii. 4 — \emph{the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Col. iii. 12 — \emph{put on therefore, as the elect of God, bowels of mercies} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Jas. v. 11 — \emph{the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Acts xvii. 30 — \emph{the times of this ignorance God winked at}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{This is a catalogue of the Names of mercy, each with its proof-text}, and the proof-texts are doing the work a lexicon would: \emph{bonitas} from Samuel, \emph{charitas} from Romans, \emph{hominum dilectio} from Titus — the Greek φιλανθρωπία — down to the \emph{viscera} of James. The page is closer to a concordance than to a prayer, and it is the ground the next page prays from.}

\enleafn{110}{\input{fragments/en110}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. v. 2 — \emph{where sin abounded, grace did much more abound}, which is verse 20 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. ii. 4 — \emph{the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Tim. ii. 25 — \emph{if God peradventure will give them repentance} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Pet. i. 19 — \emph{the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Acts iv. 12 — \emph{none other name under heaven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxix. 5 — \emph{my sins are not hid from thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxxviii. 9 — \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{The plate cites \textup{Rom. v. 2}, and the verse is Rom. v. 20.} \emph{Superabundavit gratia} is the Vulgate of Romans v. 20 word for word; v. 2 is \emph{access by faith into this grace}, a different sentence. \textbf{And the volume proves it against itself}: printed 103 cites \textup{Rom. v. 20} correctly. A dropped nought, kept as printed — the fifth place in this edition where one page corrects another.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{Two verses of the same shape, set one under the other.} \emph{My sins are not hid from thee} and \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee} are different psalms — lxix and xxxviii — and Andrewes has put them together for the repeated clause, which is how most of this book is built. The English keeps both, unvaried, so the repetition reads as the design it is.}

\enleafn{114}{\input{fragments/en114}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Gal. iii. 10 — \emph{cursed is every one that continueth not in all things} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,1 Cor. xv. 56 — \emph{the sting of death is sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Cor. xv. 20 — \emph{the firstfruits of them that slept} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Heb. vii. 25 — \emph{he ever liveth to make intercession for them} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Rom. ii. 6 — \emph{who will render to every man according to his deeds} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Luke xxiv. 49 — \emph{until ye be endued with power from on high}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{The Creed again, but each article answered by what it did.} Not \emph{he was crucified} but the cross taking away the curse of the law; not \emph{he rose} but the firstfruits; not \emph{he sitteth} but the appearing and interceding. \enleafn{130}{\input{fragments/en130}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xc. 14 — \emph{O satisfy us early with thy mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 20 — \textbf{the work of the fifth day}: the moving creature that hath life \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxlviii. 10 — \emph{creeping things, and flying fowl} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Gen. i. 22 — \emph{be fruitful, and multiply} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cviii. 5 — \emph{thy glory above all the earth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Col. iii. 2 — \emph{set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth}\par}}

\markright{134}
\setnoted{3,5,7,12,22,27,29}
\enleafn{134}{\input{fragments/en134}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Jas. iii. 2 — \emph{in many things we offend all} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jas. ii. 13 — \emph{judgment without mercy to him that hath shewed no mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 John i. 8 — \emph{if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 John ii. 1 — \emph{we have an advocate with the Father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxxvii. 7 — \emph{will the Lord cast off for ever?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Heb. xii. 1 — \emph{the sin which doth so easily beset us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Jas. i. 21 — \emph{superfluity of naughtiness}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{He doubles the preposition, and the doubling is the argument.} \emph{Advocatum ad te apud te habeo} — an advocate \textbf{to} thee and \textbf{with} thee: the one pleaded before is the one pleaded to, and both are God. It is the court figure the book keeps returning to, and the English holds both prepositions rather than smoothing them into one.}

\setnoted{1,6,25,26,27,28,30,32}
\enleafn{136}{\input{fragments/en136}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 John ii. 16 — \emph{the pride of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. v. 3 — \emph{blessed are the poor in spirit; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. xi. 6 — \emph{a rewarder of them that diligently seek him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Job xix. 25 — \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xvi. 16 — Peter at Cæsarea Philippi: \emph{thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,John iv. 42 — the Samaritans: \emph{this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Acts xv. 11 — Peter at the council: \emph{we shall be saved, even as they}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{Three confessions in a row, and not one of them from the same quarter.} Job's \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} comes from outside Israel altogether; Peter's \emph{thou art the Christ} from the chief of the apostles; the Samaritans' \emph{this is indeed the Saviour of the world} from foreigners who had believed on the word of a woman. Andrewes sets them one under another without comment, and the arrangement says what no one of them says alone.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{138}{\input{fragments/en138}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xix. 25 — the verse continuing: \emph{whom I shall see for myself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxvii. 15 — \emph{to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxxiii. 20 — \emph{our soul waiteth for the LORD} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxxiii. 21 — \emph{let thy mercy be upon us, according as we hope in thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,⚠ \textbf{\textup{Psal. xxvii. 15} is not an error: it is the Prayer Book's numbering.} The Authorised Version has this verse at xxvii. 13; the BCP Psalter, which divides the psalm differently, has it at 15 — and the BCP is the book Andrewes had to hand, as printed 433 shows twice over. \textbf{Do not "correct" it.} The volume moves between the two numberings without warning, and only reading the verse tells you which is in use.}

\sethead{The Sixth Day}
% ---------- opening 148 | 149 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{148}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Day}
\originals{148}{\input{fragments/gr148}}{\input{fragments/la149}}
\clearpage
\markright{148}
\setnoted{3,6,9,12,13,14,16,17,18}
\enleafn{148}{\input{fragments/en148}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxxviii. 13 — \emph{in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 25 — \textbf{the work of the sixth day}: the beast of the earth after his kind \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{let us make man in our image} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — the divine hand set to its own work \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Gen. ii. 7 — \emph{and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. viii. 6 — \emph{thou madest him to have dominion} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xci. 11 — \emph{he shall give his angels charge over thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Gen. ii. 8 — \emph{and the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{Seven dignities in the making of man, counted out.} A deliberation held beforehand, the divine hand set to the work, the breath of life, the image, dominion over the works, angels given charge, and a garden — each with its text. Andrewes is not retelling Genesis i but \emph{itemising} it, and the sixth day's prayer is built on the count: what man was made with is the ground of everything the page goes on to ask.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{150}{\input{fragments/en150}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,2 Pet. i. 4 — \emph{partakers of the divine nature} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the promise of the seed that should bruise the serpent \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gal. iv. 4 — \emph{when the fulness of the time was come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Hos. xiii. 16 — the prophet's word of a people fallen by its own iniquity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Hos. xiv. 1 — \emph{so will we render the calves of our lips}, which is verse 2 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Joel ii. 17 — \emph{give not thine heritage to reproach}\par}}

\setnoted{8}
\originalsn{152}{\input{fragments/gr152}}{\input{fragments/la153}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,8 \emph{Græca om. apogr., quæ Hebraice leguntur}: \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} (\emph{Ion.} ii. 7), \emph{sub titulo} \textup{Τοῦ Ἰωνᾶ}}{}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{152}
\setnoted{1,3,8,25,26,30}
\enleafn{152}{\input{fragments/en152}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Amos vii. 5 — Amos staying the judgment: \emph{O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jonah ii. 8 — \emph{they that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Zech. iii. 3 — Joshua the high priest in filthy garments, and Satan at his right hand \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Zech. ix. 11 — \emph{by the blood of thy covenant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. li. 2 — \emph{cleanse me from my sin}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,⚠ \textbf{Here the manuscript reads HEBREW where the printed page reads Greek.} The apograph gives \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} — Jonah ii. 7, \emph{thou hast brought up my life from corruption} — under its own heading, \emph{Of Jonah}; the 1853 set the Greek instead. This is the sharpest of the thirteen places where the printed book quietly drops Andrewes' third script, because here the Hebrew is not a gloss beside the text but \textbf{the text itself}. Recorded, not restored.}
\clearpage

\markright{154}
\setnoted{2,5,9,14,16,18,19,24,25,26,29,30,32}
\enleafn{154}{\input{fragments/en154}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Zech. iii. 2 — \emph{is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xxiii. 34 — \emph{Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts vii. 60 — Stephen, kneeling: \emph{lay not this sin to their charge} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke xxii. 44 — \emph{his sweat was as it were great drops of blood} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xxvii. 29 — \emph{a crown of thorns, and put it upon his head} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Heb. v. 7 — \emph{with strong crying and tears} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Matt. xxvii. 39 — \emph{they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxxix. 3 — \emph{the plowers plowed upon my back} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxii. 17 — \emph{they pierced my hands and my feet}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Matt. xxvii. 46 — \emph{Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani}, at the ninth hour \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Cor. xi. 24 — \emph{this is my body, which is broken for you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Matt. xxvi. 28 — at the Supper: \emph{my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. lxxxv. 2 — \emph{thou hast covered all their sin}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textbf{The Passion assembled out of five books, and not one of them a Gospel narrative of it.} The bloody sweat and the strong crying come from Luke and Hebrews, but the plowed back, the pierced hands and feet and the covered sin come from the Psalms, and the broken body from an epistle about a supper. Andrewes builds the scene from texts that are not describing it, which is why the sequence reads as prayer and not as recital.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{158}{\input{fragments/en158}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Cor. xii. 8 — the gifts of the Spirit, severally divided \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — \emph{forsake not the works of thine own hands} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{because} in thine image and likeness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Rev. v. 9 — \emph{because} thou hast redeemed me by thy blood \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. iii. 5 — \emph{because} of the washing of regeneration \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. xi. 17 — \emph{because} thou hast graffed me into the good olive tree \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Eph. v. 30 — \emph{because} a member of his body\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,*\emph{Five pleas, and every one of them begins }Quia\emph{.}* The prayer does not ask on the ground of need but on the ground of fact — because I am in thine image, because thou hast bought me, because thou hast washed me, because thou hast graffed me in, because I am a member. The repeated conjunction is the argument, and the English keeps it at the head of each line rather than varying it for elegance.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{172}{\input{fragments/en172}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. viii. 8 — the centurion: \emph{speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. viii. 25 — the disciples in the storm: \emph{Lord, save us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Mark iv. 38 — \emph{carest thou not that we perish?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. ix. 2 — to the man sick of the palsy: \emph{thy sins be forgiven thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xvii. 13 — the ten lepers, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Mark x. 47 — blind Bartimæus by the wayside \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Mark vii. 34 — to the deaf man: \emph{Ephphatha, that is, Be opened} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Luke xiii. 12 — to the bowed woman: \emph{thou art loosed from thine infirmity} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxxv. 3 — \emph{say unto my soul, I am thy salvation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my grace is sufficient for thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,*\emph{The whole page is one request, asked ten times: }say it to me\emph{.}\emph{ Andrewes goes through the Gospels collecting the words Christ spoke to particular people — }be opened\emph{ to the deaf man, }thou art loosed\emph{ to the bowed woman, }thy sins be forgiven thee\emph{ to the palsied, }my grace is sufficient* to Paul — and asks for each of them in the first person. He is not recalling the miracles; he is asking to be the one they were said to. The Psalm and the Epistle at the foot are admitted on the same terms, as words spoken to somebody.}

\setnoted{3,20}
\enleafn{184}{\input{fragments/en184}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rev. xix. 5 — \emph{praise our God, all ye his servants, both small and great} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rev. xxi. 4 — \emph{for the former things are passed away}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,⚠ \textbf{The manuscript has its largest silence immediately after this line.} Andrewes' own book leaves \textbf{three blank leaves} here — six blank pages, more than it leaves anywhere else — and the next thing in it is the great personal intercession that the 1853 prints on the following leaf. The printed page runs straight on. What the blank leaves mean is not settled: they may mark the end of the seven days, or room left for matter never written. \textbf{Nothing has been re-cut on the strength of them}; the division is recorded here and in \textup{apparatus/CLASS-B-unit-boundaries.md}, which is where a decision about it would have to be argued.}

\enleafn{204}{\input{fragments/en204}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Acts xii. 22 — Herod hailed as a god, and eaten of worms \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts xxiv. 27 — Felix, \emph{willing to shew the Jews a pleasure} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Sam. vi. 16 — Michal despising David as he danced before the ark \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Sam. ii. 13 — the fleshhook of Hophni, taking the priests' portion by force \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Kings xi. 1 — Athaliah destroying all the seed royal \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Acts viii. 18 — Simon offering money for the gift; Matt. xxvi. 16 — Judas, from the thirty pieces, seeking his opportunity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Tim. iii. 6 — \emph{not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Hos. iv. 4 — \emph{this people are as they that strive with the priest} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,2 Sam. xv. 31 — Ahithophel's counsel, prayed into foolishness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Kings xxi. 15 — the judges of Jezreel, and Naboth's vineyard \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Num. xxv. 5 — the plague at Baal-peor \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Josh. vii. 26 — the valley of Achor, where Achan was stoned\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,\textbf{This page names disasters by a single figure and expects the story to come with it.} \emph{Hophni's fleshhook}, \emph{Michal's contempt}, \emph{Athaliah's plundering}, \emph{Ahithophel's counsel}, \emph{the judges of Jezreel}, \emph{the torrents of Belial}, \emph{the plague of Peor}, \emph{the valley of Achor} — each is one or two words standing for a whole history, and the deprecation works only if the reader supplies it. Nowhere else in the volume does so much depend on knowing what a name is for; without the notes below, the English of this page is a list of proper nouns.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{210}{\input{fragments/en210}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xii. 28 — \emph{let us serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Cor. vi. 1 — \emph{that ye receive not the grace of God in vain} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. xii. 15 — \emph{lest any man fail of the grace of God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. iv. 14 — \emph{neglect not the gift that is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gal. v. 4 — \emph{ye are fallen from grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,2 Tim. i. 6 — \emph{stir up the gift of God which is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,2 Pet. iii. 18 — \emph{grow in grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Thess. iii. 10 — \emph{might perfect that which is lacking in your faith} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Luke xvii. 5 — \emph{increase our faith}; Heb. iii. 6 — \emph{the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Isa. xlii. 3 — \emph{the smoking flax shall he not quench} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Rom. v. 5 — \emph{the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Jas. iv. 6 — \emph{he giveth grace unto the humble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. lxxxvi. 11 — \emph{unite my heart to fear thy name}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Seven verbs of grace in seven lines, and they make a single argument.} Not to receive it in vain, not to fail of it, not to neglect it, not to fall from it — then to stir it up, to grow in it, to continue in it. Four negatives and three positives, each with its own epistle, mounting from the least a man can do to the most. The English keeps them as seven separate lines because the ladder is the point.}
\clearpage

\markright{224}
\setnoted{2,4,8,12,15,19,20,22,23,25,27}
\enleafn{224}{\input{fragments/en224}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xlii. 10 — \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lxiii. 5 — \emph{I will lift up my hands in thy Name}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxli. 2 — \emph{the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Job xxxv. 10 — \emph{God my maker, who giveth songs in the night} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Isa. xxxviii. 12 — Hezekiah again: \emph{from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ecclus. v. 5 — \emph{add not sin unto sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Prov. xxiv. 16 — \emph{a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xviii. 22 — \emph{until seventy times seven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. v. 30 — \emph{a wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Isa. xxx. 15 — \emph{in returning and rest shall ye be saved} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Deut. xxx. 2 — \emph{and shalt return unto the LORD thy God with all thine heart}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,⚠ \textbf{\textup{Psal. xlii. 10} is the Prayer Book's figure, not a slip.} The Authorised Version has \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} at xlii. \textbf{8}; the BCP Psalter numbers it 10. The same verse is cited the same way at printed \textbf{433}, four hundred pages later — so the book is consistent in this, and it is further evidence that the Prayer Book Psalter was physically to hand. \textbf{Do not correct it.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,\textbf{Two sevens, set against each other.} \emph{A just man falleth seven times} is the measure of a day's failure; \emph{until seventy times seven} is the measure of the forgiveness asked for it. Andrewes puts them two lines apart and lets the arithmetic do the work — the second number is not merely larger, it is the first one multiplied, which is the point Christ was making to Peter.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{226}{\input{fragments/en226}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. cxxx. 1 — \emph{out of the depths have I cried unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xli. 4 — \emph{heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. li. 1 — \emph{blot out mine iniquity} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxv. 16 — \emph{O bring thou me out of my troubles}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xix. 12 — secret faults, and the Septuagint's \emph{strange sins} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Wisd. iv. 12 — \emph{the wandering of concupiscence doth undermine the simple mind} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Matt. xii. 36 — \emph{every idle word that men shall speak}\par}}

\enleafn{228}{\input{fragments/en228}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Hos. xiii. 9 — \emph{O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. ciii. 10 — \emph{nor rewarded us according to our iniquities} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. lxxix. 9 — \emph{for the glory of thy name} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xiii. 3 — \emph{lest I sleep the sleep of death} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xci. 6 — the Vulgate's \emph{business that walketh in darkness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxxi. 4 — \emph{he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cvi. 4 — \emph{visit me with thy salvation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Job xxxiii. 15 — \emph{in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men}\par}}

\enleafn{230}{\input{fragments/en230}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxxviii. 7 — \emph{my loins are filled with a loathsome disease} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xvi. 8 — \emph{my reins chasten me in the night-season}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. ciii. 14 — \emph{he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xvii. 8 — \emph{hide me under the shadow of thy wings} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxxii. 7 — \emph{in a time when thou mayest be found}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxiii. 1 — \emph{early will I seek thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{The psalm the volume mis-numbered at printed 92 stands here correctly as \textup{lxiii. 1}} — the third page to give it right, after 106. The book's own consistency is what convicts the one page that differs.}
\clearpage

\markright{234}
\setnoted{}

\clearpage
\markright{234}
\setnoted{12,15,17,18,19,20,22,26}
\enleafn{234}{\input{fragments/en234}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxxi. 6 — \emph{O LORD God of truth}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. xxxiii. 5 — Jacob to Esau: \emph{the children which God hath graciously given} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 1 — \emph{thou knowest my down-sitting and mine up-rising}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxi. 8 — \emph{from this time forth, and even for evermore} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxiii. 6 — \emph{when I remember thee upon my bed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxxvii. 6 — \emph{my spirit made diligent search} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 18 — \emph{when I awake, I am still with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. iv. 8 — \emph{thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textbf{\textup{Ad scopandum spiritum meum} — he keeps the spade.} Ps. lxxvii. 6's \emph{my spirit made diligent search} is, in the Greek Andrewes used, a verb of digging over the ground; the evening examination is a turning of the soil, not a rummage. The same figure governs §41 in Part II, where the day's review is a \textbf{recall} of stragglers rather than a reveille. The English holds the spade in both places.}

% ---------- opening 240 | 241 ----------

\setnoted{}
\originals{240}{\input{fragments/gr240}}{\input{fragments/la241}}
\clearpage
\markright{240}
\setnoted{16,22,23,24,25,27,28,29,30,31,32}
\enleafn{240}{\input{fragments/en240}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. ix. 33 — \emph{whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts ii. 42 — \emph{they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xxii. 19 — \emph{this do in remembrance of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Cor. xi. 26 — \emph{ye do shew the Lord's death till he come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,1 Cor. x. 16 — \emph{the communion of the body of Christ} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. xxvi. 28 — \emph{shed for many for the remission of sins} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Cor. v. 7 — \emph{Christ our passover is sacrificed for us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xi. 28 — \emph{come unto me, and I will give you rest} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Col. ii. 14 — \emph{blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Heb. ix. 14 — \emph{purge your conscience from dead works} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Pet. ii. 24 — \emph{by whose stripes ye were healed}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Thirty-four names for one thing, each with its text.} From here to the foot of the next leaf Andrewes sets out what the Sacrament \emph{is} — the token of the assembly, the memorial of the dispensation, the shewing of the death, the communion of body and blood, the remission of sins, an amulet against all that is unlucky, the quiet of conscience, the cancelling of debts — and gives every name a proof. \textbf{It is a definition by accumulation}: no one of the names is the definition, and the list does not resolve into a doctrine. That is why the page can be read by anyone who holds any of the doctrines, and why it was worth an entire meditation.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{2,6,8,9}
\enleafn{250}{\input{fragments/en250}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Mark x. 17 — the rich young ruler: \emph{what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts ii. 37 — at Pentecost: \emph{men and brethren, what shall we do?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts xvi. 30 — the gaoler at Philippi: \emph{what must I do to be saved?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke iii. 10 — to the Baptist, three times over: \emph{what shall we do then?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{Four askings of one question, and the answers differ every time.} \emph{What shall I do?} is put by the rich young ruler, by the crowd at Pentecost, by the gaoler at Philippi, and three times over to the Baptist by the people, the publicans and the soldiers — and Scripture answers \emph{keep the commandments}, \emph{repent and be baptized}, \emph{believe on the Lord Jesus}, and a different practical charge to each trade. Andrewes sets them together without reconciling them.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{258}{\input{fragments/en258}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Tit. iii. 11 — \emph{condemned of himself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxliii. 2 — \emph{enter not into judgment with thy servant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Pet. v. 6 — \emph{humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Eph. iii. 14 — \emph{I bow my knees unto the Father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xxvi. 39 — in the garden: \emph{let this cup pass from me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxliii. 6 — \emph{I stretch forth my hands unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican smote upon his breast; Jer. xxxi. 19 — Ephraim smote upon his thigh \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxxx. 1 — \emph{out of the depths have I cried} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxxv. 10 — \emph{all my bones shall say, LORD, who is like unto thee?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. ciii. 1 — \emph{all that is within me, bless his holy name}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vii}\,\textbf{Two men striking themselves, and Andrewes takes both.} The publican in the Gospel \emph{smote upon his breast}; Ephraim in Jeremiah \emph{smote upon my thigh}. The brace on the page offers the reader either, and the two references stand side by side because neither gesture is the right one — the point is that repentance has a body, and Scripture shows it more than one way to move.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{260}{\input{fragments/en260}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. vi. 2 — \emph{have mercy upon me, O LORD; for I am weak} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. lxxviii. 39 — \emph{a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Isa. xl. 6 — \emph{all flesh is grass} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. ciii. 16 — \emph{the place thereof shall know it no more} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Gen. xviii. 27 — Abraham pleading for Sodom: \emph{I am but dust and ashes} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Job xvii. 14 — \emph{I have said to corruption, Thou art my father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xxxix. 14 — \emph{I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Job iv. 19 — \emph{them that dwell in houses of clay} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Gen. xlvii. 9 — Jacob before Pharaoh: \emph{few and evil have the days of the years of my life been} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Isa. xxxviii. 13 — Hezekiah: \emph{from morning even to night wilt thou make an end of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Job xiv. 1 — \emph{of few days, and full of trouble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. lxxiv. 18 — \emph{remember this, that the enemy hath reproached}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,⚠ \textbf{The same clause, two verse-numbers, three hundred pages apart.} \emph{Memorare quæ mea substantia} is referred here to \textup{Psal. lxxxix. 47} and at printed \textbf{35} to \textup{lxxxix. 46}. The Authorised Version has it at \textbf{47}, so the earlier page is the one that slipped. \textbf{Both kept as printed} — this is the seventh place where the volume settles one of its own references by citing it correctly elsewhere.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{262}{\input{fragments/en262}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxx. 9 — \emph{what profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. li. 1 — \emph{according to the multitude of thy tender mercies} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Eph. i. 7 — \emph{the riches of his grace}; Eph. i. 8 — \emph{wherein he hath abounded toward us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Dan. ix. 19 — \emph{defer not, for thine own sake, O my God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,John xiv. 13 — \emph{whatsoever ye shall ask in my name} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Jas. ii. 13 — \emph{mercy rejoiceth against judgment} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Dan. ix. 19 — the same verse closing the Meditation as it opened the plea\par}}

\sethead{§2 \emph{Preces Matutinæ}}
% ---------- printed 270 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{270}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§2 \emph{Preces Matutinæ}}
\originalsone{270}{\input{fragments/la270}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{270}
\setnoted{2,5,7,9,11,21,23}
\enleafn{270}{\input{fragments/en270}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxv. 2 — \emph{O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lv. 17 — \emph{evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. v. 3 — \emph{my voice shalt thou hear in the morning} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxli. 2 — \emph{let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxiii. 7 — \emph{because thou hast been my help} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxxiii. 2 — \emph{until that he have mercy upon us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxix. 132 — \emph{as thou usest to do unto those that love thy name}\par}}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 271 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{271}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{271}{\input{fragments/la271}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{271}
\setnoted{2,4,6,8,15,16,17,20,24,26,28}
\enleafn{271}{\input{fragments/en271}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xci. 11 — \emph{he shall give his angels charge over thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxv. 4 — \emph{teach me thy paths} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxix. 133 — \emph{let not any iniquity have dominion over me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xvii. 5 — \emph{that my footsteps slip not} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. iii. 4 — the Greek word Andrewes keeps, φιλάνθρωπε, \emph{the love of God toward man} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Jas. v. 11 — πολυεύσπλαγχνος, \emph{the Lord is very pitiful} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,2 Cor. i. 3 — \emph{the Father of mercies} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Luke xv. 19 — the prodigal: \emph{no more worthy to be called thy son} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Mark ix. 24 — \emph{help thou mine unbelief} — here made \emph{help thou mine impenitence} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Luke i. 78 — \emph{through the tender mercy of our God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Eph. i. 7 — \emph{according to the riches of his grace}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ix}\,\textbf{He alters the verse as he prays it, and the alteration is the petition.} The father in Mark cries \emph{help thou mine unbelief}; Andrewes writes \emph{adjuva Tu impœnitentiam meam} — help thou mine \textbf{impenitence}. The substitution is deliberate and is not a misquotation: what he wants help against is not doubt but hardness. The English keeps his word and the note keeps the Gospel's, because the reader needs to hear both to hear either.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 272 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{272}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{272}{\input{fragments/la272}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{272}
\setnoted{3,4,5,6,8,9,10,14,17,18}
\enleafn{272}{\input{fragments/en272}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Eph. ii. 4 — \emph{for his great love wherewith he loved us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — \emph{God be merciful to me a sinner} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xlii. 7 — \emph{deep calleth unto deep} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Rom. v. 20 — \emph{where sin abounded, grace did much more abound} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. xii. 21 — \emph{overcome evil with good} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Jas. ii. 13 — \emph{mercy rejoiceth against judgment} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xvi. 16 — \emph{thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,John i. 29 — \emph{behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Luke xix. 10 — \emph{to seek and to save that which was lost}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{v}\,\textbf{\textup{Rom. v. 20} again, and cited right.} This is the third page to give the verse correctly — with printed 103 and 111's own facing evidence — against the \textup{Rom. v. 2} at printed 111. ⚠ And note what he does with it: the Vulgate's indicative \emph{superabundavit gratia}, grace \textbf{did} abound, becomes the subjunctive \emph{superabundet}, let it abound. He turns a statement of what happened into a request that it happen again.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§3 \emph{Intercessio}}
% ---------- printed 273 ----------

\markright{273}
\setnoted{6,18,20}
\enleafn{273}{\input{fragments/en273}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Tit. i. 5 — \emph{set in order the things that are wanting} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Tim. ii. 15 — ὀρθοτομεῖν, \emph{rightly dividing}; Gal. ii. 14 — \emph{walked not uprightly} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. xii. 3 — \emph{not to think of himself more highly than he ought}\par}}

\markright{274}
\setnoted{6,23,25,26}
\enleafn{274}{\input{fragments/en274}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. cxvii. 25 — \emph{save now, I beseech thee} — the Hosanna, on the Vulgate's numbering of the psalm; the page sets it in Hebrew too \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lxxix. 13 — \emph{render unto our neighbours seven-fold into their bosom}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxv. 12 — \emph{his seed shall inherit the land}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xli. 1 — \emph{blessed is he that considereth the poor}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textbf{The Hosanna stands here in Hebrew on the printed page} — \textup{\RL{הצליחה נא}}, \emph{hoshi'ah-na}, Ps. cxviii. 25 — one of the few places the 1853 let Andrewes' third script through. It is the cry the crowds took up on Palm Sunday, and he uses it as the hinge of the intercession: the word is a petition (\emph{save now}) before it is an acclamation.}
\clearpage

\sethead{§4 \emph{Gratiarum Actio}}
% ---------- printed 276 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{276}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§4 \emph{Gratiarum Actio}}
\originalsone{276}{\input{fragments/la276}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{276}
\setnoted{5,7,8,11,13,16,17,19,20,22,24,26}
\enleafn{276}{\input{fragments/en276}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. iv. 17 — \emph{calleth those things which be not as though they were} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Col. i. 16 — \emph{visible and invisible} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. i. 3 — \emph{upholding all things by the word of his power} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Acts xiv. 17 — \emph{filling our hearts with food and gladness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxix. 91 — \emph{for all are thy servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Gen. ii. 7 — \emph{the breath of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{in our image, after our likeness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. viii. 6 — \emph{thou madest him to have dominion} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Gen. ii. 15 — \emph{and put him into the garden of Eden} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Acts xi. 18 — \emph{granted repentance unto life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the promised seed; 2 Pet. i. 4 — \emph{partakers of the divine nature} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Rom. i. 19 — \emph{that which may be known of God}\par}}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 277 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{277}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{277}{\input{fragments/la277}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{277}
\setnoted{3,5,7,10,13,15,16,17,21,23,28}
\enleafn{277}{\input{fragments/en277}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Gal. iv. 4 — \emph{when the fulness of the time was come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Heb. ii. 16 — \emph{he took on him the seed of Abraham} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Phil. ii. 7 — \emph{took upon him the form of a servant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Eph. v. 2 — \emph{an offering and a sacrifice to God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gal. iii. 13 — \emph{made a curse for us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Isa. v. 4 — the vineyard: \emph{what could have been done more?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,2 Pet. i. 4 — \emph{partakers of the divine nature} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Cor. ii. 14 — \emph{the savour of his knowledge} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,1 Pet. iii. 2 — \emph{your chaste conversation coupled with fear} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Heb. xi. 37 — of those who suffered \emph{even unto blood} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Heb. ix. 15 — \emph{they which are called might receive the promise}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,⚠ \textbf{Isaiah's question is asked of Christ, not of Israel.} \emph{What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?} is God's complaint against a people that yielded wild grapes; Andrewes turns it into praise — \emph{nihil non faciens quo facto opus erat}, leaving nothing undone that needed doing. \textbf{The reproach becomes a commendation} by changing who is speaking of whom, and that inversion is the sort of thing his method does constantly.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 278 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{278}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{278}{\input{fragments/la278}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{278}
\setnoted{1,3,4,6,7,9,17,19,21,26,28,30}
\enleafn{278}{\input{fragments/en278}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Tim. iii. 15 — \emph{the pillar and ground of the truth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. xvi. 18 — \emph{the gates of hell shall not prevail against it} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Tim. vi. 20 — \emph{keep that which is committed to thy trust} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Col. ii. 5 — \emph{your order, and the stedfastness of your faith} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Sam. vii. 13 — \emph{I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxlvii. 14 — \emph{filleth thee with the finest of the wheat} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cv. 22 — \emph{and teach his senators wisdom} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Jer. iii. 15 — \emph{pastors which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Isa. ii. 4 — \emph{their spears into pruninghooks} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Tit. iii. 5 — \emph{the renewing of the Holy Ghost} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Wisd. xi. 23 — \emph{thou winkest at the sins of men, because they should amend} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Isa. xxx. 18 — \emph{therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you}\par}}

\enleafn{280}{\input{fragments/en280}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Isa. lxiii. 15 — \emph{look down from heaven, and behold from the habitation of thy holiness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxiii. 5 — \emph{who dwelleth on high, and humbleth himself to behold} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xliv. 1 — \emph{our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Rev. vi. 16 — \emph{hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xxv. 33 — the goats set on the left hand \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. viii. 12 — \emph{cast out into outer darkness}\par}}

\enleafn{281}{\input{fragments/en281}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rev. xiv. 11 — \emph{the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Eph. iv. 18 — \emph{the blindness of their heart} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Prov. vii. 13 — the strange woman, \emph{with an impudent face}; Isa. xlviii. 4 — \emph{thy brow brass} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. iv. 2 — \emph{conscience seared with a hot iron} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. i. 16 — \emph{unto every good work reprobate} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,1 John v. 16 — \emph{a sin unto death} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Matt. xii. 32 — the word against the Holy Ghost\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,\textbf{A soft forehead and a hard one, and both are prayed against.} Proverbs gives the \emph{impudent face} of the strange woman; Isaiah gives the brow of brass. Andrewes braces them as the two ways a face can fail — shamelessness that feels nothing and obstinacy that yields nothing — and asks to be delivered from either. The English keeps the brace rather than choosing.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{15,16,17,18,20,22}
\enleafn{282}{\input{fragments/en282}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Tim. vi. 5 — \emph{men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Hos. xi. 5 — \emph{the Assyrian shall be his king, because they refused to return} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Kings xii. 27 — Jeroboam, who feared the people would return to Jerusalem \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Kings xii. 13 — Rehoboam, who answered the people roughly \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Judg. ix. 23 — \emph{God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxx. 2 — \emph{deliver my soul from lying lips}; Ps. xci. 3 — \emph{the snare of the fowler}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textbf{Four names for four ways a people is lost, and none of them is explained.} Asshur is the foreign power a nation is given over to; Jeroboam the ruler who divides worship to keep a throne; Rehoboam the ruler who answers roughly and loses ten tribes; the evil spirit of Shechem the discord God sends between a man and his own city. As at printed 204, the deprecation depends entirely on the reader knowing the histories, and the English can only name them.}
\clearpage
